items.prompt_md: Why does halving a search range repeatedly give about log2(n) steps?
options: Each step removes exactly one element, so n steps are needed
After k halvings n / 2^k remain, and that reaches 1 when k = log2(n)
Halving costs O(log n) per step, so total is n log n
Because the range doubles each step
items.answer: After k halvings n / 2^k remain, and that reaches 1 when k = log2(n)
items.explanation_md: n / 2^k = 1 gives k = log2(n). The work per step is O(1), so the total is O(log n).

items.prompt_md: Roughly how many halving steps does it take to shrink a range of 10^9 down to one item?
options: About 30
About 1,000
About 31,000
About 10^9
items.answer: About 30
items.explanation_md: 2^30 is just over 10^9, so about 30 halvings. That is why O(log n) is considered nearly free.

items.prompt_md: A grid has m rows and n columns, and you visit every cell once. Which is the correct complexity?
options: O(n^2), treating the larger of m and n as n
O(m + n)
O(log(m * n))
O(m * n)
items.answer: O(m * n)
items.explanation_md: Two independent dimensions multiply for a full scan. Collapsing both into one n is only valid if the grid is square, and you should say so.

items.prompt_md: Why is a staircase walk from the top-right of a row- and column-sorted matrix O(m + n)?
options: It binary searches each row, costing log n per row
It visits every cell exactly once
Each step moves left or down, discarding a row or column, so at most m + n steps are taken
It sorts the matrix first
items.answer: Each step moves left or down, discarding a row or column, so at most m + n steps are taken
items.explanation_md: Each move eliminates one row or one column. You can move at most m times down and n times left, so m + n steps.

items.prompt_md: BFS or DFS over a graph with V vertices and E edges, using an adjacency list, runs in:
options: O(V * E)
O(V + E), since each vertex and each edge is processed a constant number of times
O(V^2) always
O(E log V) always
items.answer: O(V + E), since each vertex and each edge is processed a constant number of times
items.explanation_md: Each vertex is dequeued once and each adjacency entry is scanned once. V * E or V^2 would only fit different representations.

items.prompt_md: Sorting n strings that each have length k costs about O(n * k * log n). Why is the k there?
options: Each of the O(n log n) comparisons may compare up to k characters
Sorting makes k passes over the data
Each string is copied k times in memory
The k comes from the number of distinct strings
items.answer: Each of the O(n log n) comparisons may compare up to k characters
items.explanation_md: Comparing two strings is O(k) in the worst case. Ignoring k would hide real work.

items.prompt_md: Walking an n-sized array while maintaining a heap capped at size k costs:
options: O(n log n), since the heap holds n items
O(k log n)
O(n + k)
O(n log k), since each of n items does a heap operation costing log k
items.answer: O(n log k), since each of n items does a heap operation costing log k
items.explanation_md: The heap never holds more than k items, so each push or pop is O(log k). Using n would overstate the cost.

items.prompt_md: A problem says n is at most 20. Which complexity is typically acceptable?
options: Only O(log n)
Only O(n)
Exponential, such as O(2^n) or O(n * 2^n)
Nothing above O(n log n)
items.answer: Exponential, such as O(2^n) or O(n * 2^n)
items.explanation_md: 2^20 is about a million, which is fine. A tiny n is the hint that enumerating all subsets is intended.

items.prompt_md: A problem has n up to 10^5. Which target complexity does this suggest?
options: O(n^2) is fine at this size
About O(n log n) or better, since O(n^2) means roughly 10^10 operations
Only O(2^n) will work
Only O(1) will work
items.answer: About O(n log n) or better, since O(n^2) means roughly 10^10 operations
items.explanation_md: At about 10^8 simple operations per second, 10^10 is far too slow. n log n is about 1.7 million, comfortable.

items.prompt_md: `my_sqrt(x)` binary searches [0, x] for the largest r with r*r <= x. What are its time and space?
options: O(log x) time and O(1) space
O(sqrt x) time and O(1) space
O(log x) time and O(log x) space
O(x) time and O(1) space
items.answer: O(log x) time and O(1) space
items.explanation_md: The range halves each step with O(1) work, and only lo, hi and mid are stored.

items.prompt_md: Trying r = 1, 2, 3, ... until r*r exceeds x takes how long?
options: O(log x)
O(x)
O(sqrt x), since r stops near the square root
items.answer: O(sqrt x), since r stops near the square root
items.explanation_md: The loop runs about sqrt(x) times. It is far better than O(x) but still far worse than halving the search range.

items.prompt_md: Counting negatives in an m-by-n matrix whose rows and columns are sorted, using the staircase walk, takes:
options: O(m * n) time and O(1) space
O(m log n) time and O(m) space
O(m + n) time and O(1) space
O(log(m * n)) time and O(1) space
items.answer: O(m + n) time and O(1) space
items.explanation_md: Each step discards a row or column. A full scan is O(m * n); binary searching each row would give O(m log n), valid but slower than the staircase for tall matrices.

items.prompt_md: Checking whether n is a power of two by repeatedly halving it while it is even takes how long?
options: O(n) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(1) space
O(sqrt n) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(log n) space
items.answer: O(log n) time and O(1) space
items.explanation_md: Each division by two removes one bit, so at most log2(n) iterations. Only a few variables: constant space.

items.prompt_md: Find the integer square root of a number up to 2 * 10^9 without a built-in, in a few dozen steps.
options: Binary search on the answer, since r*r is monotonic in r
Try every r starting from 1
Memoize the squares of all numbers
Backtrack through candidate roots
items.answer: Binary search on the answer, since r*r is monotonic in r
items.explanation_md: Monotonic predicates over a numeric range are the 'search the answer space' signal. Trying every r costs about 46,000 steps here, and the rest do not apply.

items.prompt_md: A matrix of m rows and n columns has each row sorted left to right and each column sorted top to bottom; count its negative numbers faster than scanning every cell.
options: Hash all cells into a set
Recursively split the matrix into four quadrants and slice copies
Sort every row again
Staircase walk from a corner, moving to discard a row or column each step
items.answer: Staircase walk from a corner, moving to discard a row or column each step
items.explanation_md: The two sort orders let one comparison eliminate a whole row or column, giving O(m + n). Hashing or re-sorting ignores the structure.

items.prompt_md: Tell whether a positive integer is a power of two in constant time, using its binary representation.
options: Loop up to sqrt(n) trying divisors
Build a set of all powers of two up to n
A bit trick such as n & (n - 1) == 0
Sort the digits of n
items.answer: A bit trick such as n & (n - 1) == 0
items.explanation_md: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so n & (n - 1) clears it to zero. It is O(1); the other options are slower or heavier.

items.prompt_md: A list has up to 2 * 10^5 integers and you need the k-th largest, with k small (at most 50).
options: Re-sort the whole list in a nested loop for every element
Keep a min-heap of size k while scanning, O(n log k)
Binary search the list immediately
Build an n by n table
items.answer: Keep a min-heap of size k while scanning, O(n log k)
items.explanation_md: A capped heap costs log k per item, which beats a full sort when k is small. It also introduces the n and k variables the lesson warned about.

items.prompt_md: A graph has V cities and E roads, and you want to know if two cities are connected, with V up to 10^5 and E up to 2 * 10^5.
options: Traverse with BFS or DFS over an adjacency list, O(V + E)
Compare every pair of cities with a nested loop, O(V^2)
Binary search the road list
Memoize the recursion on city pairs only
items.answer: Traverse with BFS or DFS over an adjacency list, O(V + E)
items.explanation_md: Connectivity is a traversal question and V + E is about 3 * 10^5 steps. A V^2 pairing is 10^10, too slow.

items.prompt_md: Constraints say the array has at most 18 elements and you must choose any subset to maximize a score.
options: Binary search on the subset size
Two pointers on a sorted array
Sliding window over the array
Enumerate subsets with backtracking or bitmasks, since 2^18 is small
items.answer: Enumerate subsets with backtracking or bitmasks, since 2^18 is small
items.explanation_md: With n at most 18, 2^18 (about 262,000) subsets can be enumerated. The small limit is the hint that exponential is intended.

items.prompt_md: Given an array of 10^5 positive numbers, find the smallest subarray length whose sum reaches a target, in about O(n).
options: Check all subarrays with nested loops
Binary search on array indices without a monotonic check
Sliding window with two pointers over positive numbers
Recurse on each prefix
items.answer: Sliding window with two pointers over positive numbers
items.explanation_md: Positive numbers make the window sum monotonic as it grows or shrinks, giving a linear pass. All pairs is O(n^2), which n of 10^5 rules out.

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted array of 10^9 possible values you can query by index, find where a target would be inserted.
options: Walk through each index until the target
Binary search for the insertion boundary
Build a hash set of the array
Sort the array first
items.answer: Binary search for the insertion boundary
items.explanation_md: Sorted plus an index lookup supports halving: O(log n), about 30 probes. Everything else touches many more items.

items.prompt_md: Constraints say n is at most 10^5 and you are tempted by a double loop over all pairs. Which approach is actually viable?
options: An O(n log n) or O(n) approach such as sorting, hashing, or a single pass
The double loop, since n^2 is small enough
An exponential search over all subsets
Rebuilding the structure from scratch per element
items.answer: An O(n log n) or O(n) approach such as sorting, hashing, or a single pass
items.explanation_md: n^2 at 10^5 is about 10^10 operations, too many. The constraint points at n log n or linear.

items.prompt_md: An array holds 10^6 sorted integers and you must report how many are strictly less than a given value, answering 10^5 such queries.
options: Scan the whole array for each query
Build a graph of the values
Backtrack through possible counts
Binary search the boundary for each query, O(log n) each
items.answer: Binary search the boundary for each query, O(log n) each
items.explanation_md: Sorted data plus many queries is a classic boundary binary search: about 20 steps per query instead of 10^6.
